Series vs. parallel battery connections: voltage (V) adds in series while capacity (mAh or Ah) stays the same, equal to the single cell's capacity. Parallel connections add capacity while voltage stays the same. Watt-hours (Wh) equal voltage times capacity, so energy scales with both. Key terms: cell capacity, nominal voltage, state of charge, cell matching, and weakest-cell limitation.

Series connection: cells share the same current path, so voltages add while capacity (mAh/Ah) stays that of one cell, assuming matched cells. Key terms: nominal voltage, capacity (mAh, Ah), watt-hours (Wh = V × Ah), energy, series vs. parallel, cell matching, balance, state of charge, BMS, runtime, C-rate.

Series-parallel battery configuration: combining series strings (which add voltage) with parallel strings (which add capacity). Key terms include nominal voltage, mAh/Ah capacity, watt-hours (energy = V×Ah), cell balancing, matched cells, internal resistance, maximum discharge current (C-rating), and BMS (battery management system) for protection.

Mismatched cell voltages cause balancing currents when cells are connected in parallel or series, which can overheat, degrade, or damage batteries, and may cause fire. Key terms include cell balancing, voltage differential, internal resistance, state of charge, overcharging, overdischarging, battery management system (BMS), and cell matching.

Jamming effectiveness depends on distance via the inverse-square law and free-space path loss: received signal strength falls off rapidly with range. SPI is a synchronous, full-duplex serial bus with a shared clock (SCK), MOSI/MISO data lines, and chip select (CS), allowing clock rates of tens of MHz. UART is asynchronous, lacks a shared clock, relies on baud-rate matching and start/stop bits, and typically runs at much lower rates. Key concepts: clock speed, throughput, latency, synchronous vs asynchronous timing, full duplex, DMA

Key concepts: UART versus SPI serial interfaces; baud rate and throughput limits; bridge or co-processor microcontroller (e.g., ESP8285 or STM32 receiver MCU) handling RF chip (SX127x/SX128x); added protocol-translation latency; packet rate and link latency in ExpressLRS; CRUSF/CRSF telemetry and channel data framing; interrupt handling, DMA, and buffering; end-to-end control latency and failsafe behavior.

ExpressLRS update rate, packet rate (e.g., 50Hz, 250Hz, 500Hz, 1000Hz), latency, control responsiveness, telemetry rate, UART baud rate and throughput limits, SPI versus UART bandwidth, CRSF protocol, channel count, failsafe timing, link quality (LQ), RSSI, interference, and tradeoffs between responsiveness and range or robustness.

SPI receivers connect the RF chip directly to the flight controller's MCU via SPI lines (MOSI, MISO, SCK, chip select), requiring firmware support and pin mapping in configurators like Betaflight or ExpressLRS Configurator. UART receivers use a simple serial TX/RX pair with inverted or non-inverted signaling, a baud rate setting, and a serial port assignment. Key terms: SPI bus, chip

Key concepts: connector retention, friction fit versus mechanical locking, vibration and crash loads, strain relief, heat-shrink or zip-tie securing, current rating (amps), polarity and anti-reverse design, JST and Deans alternatives, and bullet connector retention in airframes.

Key terms: current rating (amps), bullet connectors, polarity/keyed housing, gender, solder versus pre-wired, and anti-spark. Choice depends on application, battery voltage, and weight.

Bullet connectors (typically 3.5mm, 4mm, or 5mm gold-plated) suit motor-to-ESC links: they are low-profile, compact, and lightweight, fit tight airframes, and are easy to solder. Motors use three bare wires that can be bulleted in fixed phase order, while XT60 is bulky and mainly for battery leads. Key terms: current rating, contact resistance, phase order, gold plating, bullet diameter, heat
